title: Fully-voweled sentences I — and how to stop
objectives: Student can read a complete fully-voweled sentence in planned breath groups, deciding BEFORE she begins where she will stop.
Student can stop correctly: final ḥarakah dropped, ة read as a silent hāʾ, and a long vowel before the stop allowed to stretch.
Student can restart cleanly from the word after her stop, using the waṣl-hamzah starting vowels from 2-09.
Student can say what changed about a word when she stopped on it, in her own words.

slides.heading: Lesson 2.12 — Fully-voweled sentences I, and how to stop
A word that ends on a vowel going nowhere
body: Read 1:5, and then stop.
You will end it nastaʿīnu — with the ḍammah still sounding, hanging in the air with nothing after it.
Say that last word again, and then be silent for three seconds. You will hear it yourself.
The word ends on a vowel that is going nowhere. It sounds unfinished because it IS unfinished: no Arabic word ends in a vowel at a stop.
Everything you have read so far, you have read as if something came next. Today you learn what a word does when nothing comes next.

audio.cue: 1:5 — read it and stop. iyyāka naʿbudu wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn.
As printed: نَسْتَعِينُ, with a ḍammah — because the page is written for JOINING.
As stopped — the ḍammah gone, closing on a sukūn. This is not printed anywhere; it is what you do.

slides.heading: Why stopping is taught here, and not in Unit 3
body: This is the most important teaching decision in Unit 2, and it is a deliberate correction of the classical ordering.

There is a madd rule — the one that makes a long vowel stretch at a stop — that is DEFINED by what happens when you stop. It does not exist in joined reading at all: joined, the same word carries a plain two-count madd.

Al-Jazariyyah puts madd in chapter 11 and stopping in chapter 12. An earlier draft of this course's own syllabus inherited that order — madd at 3.18, stopping at 3.25. Both put the consequence before its cause.
So the course fixes it here. 2-12 introduces stopping, 2-13 drills it, 2-14 applies it on a real page — and Unit 3 then formalises the rule on a foundation you already have in your mouth.

At this stage stopping is a HABIT, not a taxonomy. Three things, no counts, no rule names, and no nine-item table. You meet all of that in Unit 3, and meeting it now would cost you the fluency this lesson exists to build.

slides.heading: A sentence is longer than a breath
body: Look at 105:1. Where will you breathe? Answer BEFORE you read a single word, then mark the place with a pencil arc.
This is the one habit the whole lesson is for.

The error it prevents — running out of air mid-āyah and stopping wherever the lungs give out — is the most common and the most damaging fault in early recitation, because the place the lungs choose is never a place that means anything.
The rule for now: stop at the end of an āyah, or at the end of a complete idea.
Which stops are permitted where, and what the little letters printed above the line mean, is Unit 3. Today: āyah ends are always safe. Use them.

items.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَٰبِ ٱلْفِيلِ
items.translit: alam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi-l-fīl

audio.cue: 105:1 — alam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi-l-fīl. Where does your arc go? Decide first, read second.

slides.heading: Never stop in the middle of a word
body: A word broken in half is not a word. Stopping mid-word can change the meaning, and it always changes whether what you said is Arabic at all.
If you run out of breath mid-word, the instruction is: go back to the BEGINNING of that word and read it again.
Not push through. Not resume from the middle.
This is worth drilling as its own reflex, because the panic response is to continue — and the reflex has to be stronger than the panic.

slides.heading: Stop change one — the final ḥarakah drops
body: You stop on a sukūn. Whatever vowel was on the last letter, it is gone.
نَسْتَعِينُ becomes نَسْتَعِينْ. ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ becomes ٱلْعَٰلَمِينْ. ٱلرَّحِيمِ becomes ٱلرَّحِيمْ. ٱلْفَلَقِ becomes ٱلْفَلَقْ.
Tanwīn is a ḥarakah too, so it drops the same way. أَحَدٌ becomes aḥad. لَهَبٍ becomes lahab.

The one that LOOKS different is tanwīn fatḥ — أَفْوَاجًا becomes afwājā — but look at the page: the alif is already printed there. You are not adding anything. You are reading what is written, now that the tanwīn above it has gone quiet.
That is a footnote to one rule, not a fourth rule. It costs ten seconds and saves you a rule.

audio.cue: Joined: nastaʿīnu.
Stopped: nastaʿīn.
Joined: aḥadun.
Stopped: aḥad. Tanwīn is a ḥarakah, and it drops like one.
110:2 — أَفْوَاجًا. Stopped, this is afwājā, and it is ALREADY what is printed. The alif was there all along.

slides.heading: Stop change two — ة becomes a silent hāʾ
body: The tāʾ marbūṭah ة is read as a تـ when you join, and as a هْ when you stop.
ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ becomes al-mūqadah. رَحْمَةً becomes raḥmah. مَدْرَسَةٌ becomes madrasah.
Point at the two dots on the ة: the dots are there for when you JOIN. Stop, and you ignore them.
The contrast case matters. حَمَّالَةَ ٱلْحَطَبِ — you join straight through, so the ة is a t: ḥammālata-l-ḥaṭab.
And the exception, once, in passing: ذَاتَ in نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ is written with an OPEN تـ, so it would stop as dhāt. Read what is written — if the tāʾ is open, it stays a t.

audio.cue: 104:6 joined: al-mūqadatu, with the dots read.
104:6 stopped: al-mūqadah. The dots are ignored and the letter goes soft.
111:4 — حَمَّالَةَ, joined straight through into ٱلْحَطَبِ, so the ة really is a t.
111:3 — ذَاتَ has an OPEN tāʾ. Stopped it is dhāt, not dhāh.
The stopped form of an open tāʾ: still a t.

slides.heading: Stop change three — a long vowel before the stop stretches
body: Read ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ joined: the yāʾ of ٱلرَّحِيمِ gets its ordinary two counts.
Now stop on ٱلرَّحِيمْ. It gets longer. Let it.
Do not measure it. Do not count it. Just do not cut it short.
Hear the same word both ways, back to back, twice, and notice that the difference is real and is caused by the stop and nothing else.
That stretch happens because you stopped. It is not part of the word. Join onward and it disappears again.
It has a name and a number of counts, and you get both in Unit 3. Today you only have to let it happen.

audio.cue: 1:3 joined — ar-raḥmāni-r-raḥīmi. Two counts on the yāʾ, no more.
Joined: ar-raḥīmi.
Stopped: ar-raḥīm — and longer. Same word, two lengths, and the stop is the only difference.

slides.heading: Restarting is a start — so 2-09 goes live again
body: Where do you resume from? The word you stopped on, or the word before it. Never mid-phrase, and never from the middle of a word.
And the moment you restart, everything from 2-09 is live: if the word begins with ٱ, you need the starting vowel.
ٱلْفَلَقِ resumes as al-falaqi. ٱهْدِنَا resumes as ihdinā.
Do several resumes explicitly, so you feel that stopping and starting are one skill with two halves rather than two separate topics.

audio.cue: Resume on it: al-falaqi. Article → fatḥah. Not il-falaq.
Resume on it: ihdinā. Verb, present tense يَهْدِى has a kasrah → kasrah.

slides.heading: Join it, stop it
slides.instructions: I say a word twice and you give me both readings, back to back, so you hear the difference yourself. The left of each pair is joined, the right is stopped.

audio.cue: Joined: ar-raḥīmi.
Stopped: ar-raḥīm, and the yāʾ stretches.
Joined: al-mūqadatu — the dots are read.
Stopped: al-mūqadah — the dots are ignored.
Joined: aḥadun.
Stopped: aḥad — the tanwīn drops.
Joined: nastaʿīnu.
Stopped: nastaʿīn — ḥarakah gone AND the yāʾ stretches. Two changes in one word.

slides.heading: The ة gauntlet — non-Qurʾānic
slides.instructions: Read each one twice: once joined into a following word, once stopping on it. The dots come and go. Non-Qurʾānic on purpose — a ة you can recite is not a ة you have read.

audio.cue: Joined: raḥmatan. Stopped: raḥmah.
Joined: madrasatun. Stopped: madrasah.
Joined: shajaratun. Stopped: shajarah.
Joined: ḥadīqatun. Stopped: ḥadīqah.
Joined: sayyāratun. Stopped: sayyārah — and hold the doubled yāʾ either way.
Joined: mudarrisatun. Stopped: mudarrisah.

slides.heading: The eight sentences, in order
slides.instructions: Plan first, read second. Before you make any sound, put a pencil arc over each group you will say in one breath. If you have to breathe somewhere you did not mark, we stop and re-mark it — we do not carry on.

audio.cue: 1 (113:2) — already ends on a fatḥah. Drop it: khalaq.
2 (112:1) — tanwīn ḍamm drops: aḥad.
3 (1:5) — the ḥarakah drops AND the yāʾ stretches. The reference sentence for stopping.
4 (104:6) — ة becomes a silent hāʾ: al-mūqadah.
5 (111:4) — the ة is joined as a t, then a plain stop on ٱلْحَطَبْ.
6 (111:3) — an open tāʾ that stays a t, and a tanwīn kasr dropping at the end.

grid.arabic: وَرَأَيْتَ ٱلنَّاسَ يَدْخُلُونَ فِى دِينِ ٱللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا

audio.cue: 7 (110:2) — long enough to need a planned breath, and it ends on tanwīn fatḥ.

grid.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَٰبِ ٱلْفِيلِ
grid.translit: alam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi-l-fīl

audio.cue: 8 (105:1) — the breath-plan sentence. Mark the arc before you read a word.

slides.heading: Stop on my signal
slides.instructions: Read on. When I raise my hand, stop at the END of the word you are on — not immediately, not mid-word. Finish the word, apply the changes, stop. Then resume when I lower my hand, and remember that the resume is a START.

grid.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَٰبِ ٱلْفِيلِ
grid.translit: alam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi-l-fīl

audio.cue: I will signal somewhere in here. Finish the word you are on, then stop properly.

grid.arabic: وَرَأَيْتَ ٱلنَّاسَ يَدْخُلُونَ فِى دِينِ ٱللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا

audio.cue: Longer. The signal may come twice.
If I signal here: al-fīl, with the yāʾ stretching. Then resume from the word before.
If I signal here: khalaq, the fatḥah simply gone.

slides.heading: Non-Qurʾānic sentences — the stopping is read, not remembered
slides.instructions: Every one of these ends in a ة or a tanwīn. Read each one joined into the next, then again stopping on it. This is the honest measurement: nothing here can be recited.

audio.cue: Stopped: … ila-l-madrasah. The ة goes soft.
Three ة endings in one sentence: … shajaratun kabīrah.
Stopped: … ʿala-l-lawḥah.
Stopped: … li-ṣadīqī, and the long ī at the end stretches.

slides.heading: Three things happen when you stop. Only three.

audio.cue: One — the final ḥarakah drops. Tanwīn drops with it.
Two — ة becomes a silent hāʾ. The dots were for joining.
Three — a long vowel before the stop stretches. Don't measure it; just don't cut it.
And the fourth thing, which is not a change but a consequence: your resume is a START, so the 2-09 vowels are live again.

slides.heading: Homework
tasks: Sūrat al-Fīl (105), five āyāt. Pencil your breath arcs FIRST, then read it once a day. Bring the marked copy — I check your plan, not just your reading.
The join/stop pairs, ten times each, aloud, back to back so you can hear the difference yourself.
Find five words ending in ة anywhere in the last juzʾ. Write each one twice: once as it is joined, once as it is stopped.

Read Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ (112) stopping at the end of EVERY āyah, then again joining every āyah to the next. Four āyāt, two readings. Notice that أَحَدٌ is a different sound in each. You do not have to know why yet — just notice it.

script: Read the 'why stopping is taught here' section before you teach the lesson. This lesson's position in the course is a deliberate correction of the classical ordering, and if you teach it as an ordinary sentence lesson you will lose the reason it exists.

The short version to carry into the room: the madd rule that makes a long vowel stretch at a stop is DEFINED by stopping. It does not exist in joined reading. Teaching it before stopping puts the consequence before its cause, which is what al-Jazariyyah does and what this course does not.

Open with 1:5 and let her end on nastaʿīnu with the ḍammah hanging. Then ask for three seconds of silence after it. She hears the problem herself; you supply only the sentence that names it — no Arabic word ends in a vowel at a stop.

Teach the breath plan BEFORE the three changes. Make her mark the arc on 105:1 before she makes a sound. The planning habit is what the lesson is for; the three changes are what she needs in order to execute the plan.

State the never-stop-mid-word rule flatly and give the reason, because the reason is what makes it stick. Then drill the go-back-to-the-start-of-the-word reflex, because the panic response is to push on and the reflex has to be stronger than the panic.

Three changes. Not four. Fold tanwīn into change one as a footnote and say so explicitly — it costs ten seconds and saves a rule. أَفْوَاجًا is the one that looks like an exception: show her the alif is already printed and that she is reading what is there, not adding anything.

For the ة, point at the two dots and say what they are FOR: joining. Stop, and you ignore them. Then give the contrast case حَمَّالَةَ ٱلْحَطَبِ, where she joins straight through and the ة really is a t — without it she will over-apply.
Mention ذَاتَ once, in passing. Open tāʾ, stays a t. Read what is written. Do not build a rule around it.

For change three, demonstrate ٱلرَّحِيمِ / ٱلرَّحِيمْ yourself, back to back, twice. Then refuse to name the rule or give the count. Say out loud that it has both and that Unit 3 supplies them. Planting it as an observation now is exactly why the rule will be easy later.
Do a few explicit resumes so she feels that stopping and starting are one skill with two halves. The moment she restarts, 2-09 is live — ٱلْفَلَقِ resumes as al-falaqi, not il-falaq.
Use her list from 2-11 of phrases she could not finish in one breath. This lesson is built out of that list, not out of a generic sentence set, and using it makes the connection visible to her.

Do NOT show her the full nine-item table of what changes at a stop, do not teach counts, and do not name any rule. She meets all of it in Unit 3. Meeting it now costs her the fluency this lesson exists to build.

listenFor.item: A clean, silent landing: the last letter closes, the sound stops, and there is no vowel and no breathy tail after it.
listenFor.commonMistake: The final ḥarakah is still pronounced at the stop — nastaʿīnu, al-ʿālamīna, aḥadun.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She is reading exactly what is printed, and the ḍammah IS printed. Nothing on the page tells her to drop it. This is obedience to the text, not carelessness — say so, because it is a mistake that deserves credit.
listenFor.correctionCue: The page is written for joining. When you stop, the last mark is not yours. Cut it: nastaʿīn.

listenFor.item: A soft hāʾ at every stop on a ة — al-mūqadah, raḥmah — with the two dots ignored.
listenFor.commonMistake: ة read as a t at the stop — al-mūqadat, raḥmat.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The two dots are right there, and 2-11 spent a whole lesson teaching her to read what is printed. She is also likely to have heard the -at form in ordinary spoken borrowings in her own language.
listenFor.correctionCue: Cover the two dots with your fingernail. Now what letter is it? A hāʾ. Say that — al-mūqadah — and let it be soft.

listenFor.item: The long vowel before a stop released rather than clipped — the last sound of the word being the long one.
listenFor.commonMistake: The long vowel gets cut short — nastaʿīn with a clipped yāʾ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Stopping feels like ENDING, and ending feels like hurrying. She is closing the word rather than releasing it.
listenFor.correctionCue: Hold the ee, then close. Let the last sound be the long one — don't run away from the end of the word.

listenFor.item: Stops landing where she marked them, at āyah ends or complete ideas, with the breath sized for the arc.
listenFor.commonMistake: Stopping mid-word when the breath runs out.
listenFor.whyItHappens: No plan — she started reading before deciding where she would stop. It is a planning failure, not a lung-capacity failure, and telling her to breathe more deeply will not fix it.
listenFor.correctionCue: Back to the start of that word. Now look ahead and show me where you're going to stop, before you take the breath.

listenFor.item: A resume treated as a start — the correct waṣl-hamzah vowel chosen at the restart.
listenFor.commonMistake: Resuming from the middle of a phrase, or restarting a waṣl hamzah with the wrong vowel — il-falaq.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The resume is not being treated as a START, so the 2-09 decision never gets run at all.
listenFor.correctionCue: You're starting. Which vowel? Is it ٱل? Then it's an a.

teacherNotes.homework: Daily: Sūrat al-Fīl with the breath arcs pencilled in BEFORE reading — she brings the marked copy and the PLAN is checked, not only the reading; the four join/stop pairs ten times each, back to back so she hears the difference herself; Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ read twice, once stopping at every āyah end and once joining every āyah to the next, noticing that أَحَدٌ is a different sound in each. Once in the week: five words ending in ة found anywhere in the last juzʾ, each written out twice, joined and stopped. She is told explicitly that she does not yet have to know WHY the long vowel stretches — only to let it happen and to notice that it does.
